interpretedBrief: Our 10 top-clicking Google queries for the 7 days ending 2026-11-23 plus our own research on what is missing. Research found one uncovered reader query, 'rule of 78 calculator' (3 impressions, position 64, 170/mo measured US demand, 1,000/mo for 'rule of 78'); the other nine queries are covered by existing pages or are an operator string. Build the one missing page as a free deterministic calculator that shows how the Rule of 78 allocates loan interest and what early payoff costs versus an actuarial refund.

actions.answer: Verdict/figure: the Rule of 78 front-loads interest by sum of the digits, so an early payoff refunds less unearned interest than the actuarial method; the extra cost is small on short or low-rate loans and larger on long, high-rate ones (for example $28.65 on $15,000 at 7% for 48 months paid off after 12 payments), and federal law (15 U.S.C. 1615(b)) bars it for precomputed consumer loans over 61 months.

outline.heading: Rule of 78 Calculator
outline.purpose: Opening answer sentence plus the calculator (amount, APR, term, payoff payment number); outputs Rule-of-78 refund, actuarial refund, extra interest the lender keeps.

outline.heading: How the Rule of 78 Splits Your Interest
outline.purpose: Sum-of-the-digits formula with the n(n+1)/2 denominator, a worked example from the engine, and an interest-by-month table.

outline.heading: What Early Payoff Costs Under the Rule of 78
outline.purpose: Engine cases across amount/APR/term showing when the gap is small versus large and that it falls to zero at maturity.

outline.heading: Is the Rule of 78 Legal?
outline.purpose: 15 U.S.C. 1615(b): refund must be at least as favorable as actuarial for precomputed consumer credit over 61 months consummated after Sept 30, 1993; terms of 61 months or less are not covered by that provision; state law and contract not asserted, readers told to check.

outline.heading: Who This Is Not For
outline.purpose: Simple-interest loans (most auto, personal and mortgage loans) where the Rule of 78 does not apply; business loans and non-U.S. loans.

outline.heading: What Would Change Our Answer
outline.purpose: Contract uses actuarial or simple interest; term over 61 months; state law; payoff statement shows a different refund.

outline.heading: Rule of 78 Questions
outline.purpose: FAQs in sentence case: what is it, formula, is it legal, car loan, how to get a payoff statement, vs simple interest.

newPageBriefs.contributionAndEvidence: Decision gap: readers searching the calculator cannot see the dollar cost of Rule-of-78 vs the actuarial method on their own loan. Basis calculated (own engine run, reproducible) plus reported (statute, CFPB). Provenance: scope = fixed-rate precomputed installment loan, level payments, whole months; limits = no fees, no state law, no rebate-on-default; publicMethod = on-page method note and formula. Primary sources checked 2026-11-23: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1615 (LII mirror of the U.S. Code; house.gov and govinfo 404 from runner) and https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/whats-the-difference-between-a-simple-interest-rate-and-precomputed-interest-on-an-auto-loan-en-841/ (last reviewed Jan 30, 2024). Feasibility: $15,000/7%/48 mo after 12 payments Rule 78 earns $971.99 vs actuarial $943.34 ($28.65 gap); after 42 payments $3.30; $25,000/8%/60 after 12: $88.13; $30,000/9%/72 after 24: $227.82. Counterexample: loans of 61 months or less are outside the federal ban, and at maturity the two methods agree.
newPageBriefs.tablesToolsVisuals: Calculator inputs: loan amount, APR (0-30%), term months (1-120), payoff after payment number k. Outputs: level payment (computeLoanPayment), total finance charge, Rule-of-78 interest earned and refund, actuarial interest earned and refund, difference, plus an interest-allocation-by-month table (Rule 78 vs actuarial). Formula: earned_k = total interest x sum(n-k+1..n) / (n(n+1)/2). Default preset $15,000 / 7% / 48 / 12. Inline SVG or table bar of the two refunds; static worked example readable without interaction. Phase 3c: client-side, data-tool="rule-of-78-calculator", <= ~30 KB gz, mirrors loan-payment-calculator wiring (calculators.ts entry, islandId, LIVE_IDS) with src/lib/rule-of-78.ts and a unit-tested engine.
newPageBriefs.testingAndReview: _experience.md section G excludes financial services from testing claims and this is a formula calculation, so TESTED format OFF (--tested no); no 'tested' byline or schema. Visible attribution: 'In our internal modeling, we compared the Rule of 78 with the actuarial method...' beside the first finding, with the method note nearby. Review profile expected HIGH-adjacent (statute and finance figures), independent risk assessment decides; consequential claim is the 15 U.S.C. 1615 scope statement. No professionalReviewRequired flag (explanatory, no personalized advice). Byline/Person JSON-LD template-rendered; disclaimer at page bottom only.
newPageBriefs.takeaway: Rule of 78 pushes interest into the early months, so paying a precomputed loan off early refunds less than the actuarial method would; on short or low-rate loans the extra cost is tens of dollars, on long high-rate loans it can exceed $200, and it vanishes near maturity. Federal law bars it only for precomputed consumer loans over 61 months, so a shorter precomputed loan may still use it depending on contract and state law. Applies to precomputed loans only; what would change it: a simple-interest or actuarial contract, a term over 61 months, or a payoff statement (requestable under 15 U.S.C. 1615(c), one free per year) showing a different refund. Based on our internal modeling plus the cited statute and CFPB.

reviewerGuardrails: CR-1 (substantive): In writing, label any term over 61 months as a formula illustration (a federally restricted term for precomputed consumer loans), prefer a 60-month example for the 'larger gap' case ($25,000 / 8% / 60 / 12 = $88.13, engine-computed), and make the calculator show a visible notice whenever term > 61 months. Keep the figures engine-computed, never hand-typed.

CR-2 (substantive): Writer closed fact list uses the exact subsection (b) wording above; never write 'illegal' or 'banned' without the over-61-month and precomputed-consumer conditions; do not assert any state-law position; tell readers to check the contract and request a payoff statement (1615(c): within 5 days, one free per year). Phase 4 tests this consequential claim against the 61-month counterexample.
